# S&P 500 Constituent Additions and Deletions: History and Reasons (1957–2026)

## Summary

The S&P 500 began as a 500-stock index on March 4, 1957. Since then, nearly half of deletions have occurred not because a share price fell, but because the company was acquired.

Over the 52 years from 1963 through 2014, 1,186 constituents were replaced. That is about 23 a year, meaning roughly 4–5% of the index changed each year.

Classifying 414 change records for 2007–October 2026 by reason gives 173 mergers and acquisitions (42%), 147 scheduled rebalances based on market capitalization (36%), and 51 splits or spin-offs (12%). Only six deletions involved bankruptcy or FDIC receivership.

Recent annual additions have numbered 15–19. Since 2023, a clear pattern has emerged: AI infrastructure and semiconductor companies (Super Micro, Dell, Marvell, Vertiv and Lumentum), fintech companies and private-market managers (Coinbase, Robinhood, KKR, Apollo and Ares) have entered, while smaller consumer and food-and-beverage stocks have left.

The full list of 414 change records, with reason classifications and Korean summaries, and annual totals are included in the accompanying Excel file. Public records of changes in 1957–2006 are incomplete, so that period is covered through selected examples.

## The birth of the S&P 500 and its initial composition

At launch in 1957, its 500 stocks filled sector quotas: 425 industrials, 60 utilities and 15 railroads, all listed on the New York Stock Exchange. The index was market-capitalization weighted from the outset. (Motley Fool, SAGE Encyclopedia)

| Period | Change |
| --- | --- |
| 1923 | Standard Statistics launched a weekly index of 233 stocks |
| 1926 | Reorganized into a daily composite index of 90 stocks |
| 1957-03-04 | S&P 500 launched: 425 industrials, 60 utilities and 15 railroads |
| 1976-07-01 | Reallocated to 400 industrials, 40 utilities, 20 transportation stocks and 40 financials. Disney and Anheuser-Busch joined; Houston Natural Gas and Allegheny Energy left |
| Late 1980s | Sector quotas were abandoned in favor of broader market representation |

Few of the 1957 members remain today. The current constituent list records March 4, 1957 as the addition date for 52 stocks, including 3M, IBM, Coca-Cola, P&G, GE, ExxonMobil, Boeing and Pfizer. However, this includes companies such as CVS, ConocoPhillips and Lockheed Martin that inherited the addition dates of predecessor entities. (Wikipedia constituent list)

## Addition and deletion rules

The S&P 500 does not mechanically hold the 500 companies with the largest market capitalizations. The S&P DJI index committee selects from companies meeting eligibility requirements. These are entry criteria, so an existing member is not removed immediately merely because it falls below a requirement.

(S&P DJI capitalization threshold announcement, July 1, 2025; Wikipedia S&P 1500 selection criteria)

| Item | Current criteria |
| --- | --- |
| Market capitalization | Unadjusted market capitalization of at least $22.7 billion as of July 1, 2025; float-adjusted capitalization at least 50% of that threshold |
| Profitability | Positive GAAP income from continuing operations in the latest quarter and in aggregate over the latest four quarters |
| Liquidity | Annual traded value / float-adjusted capitalization above 0.75; at least 250,000 shares traded in each of the previous six months |
| Investable weight factor (IWF) | At least 0.10 |
| IPO seasoning | 12 months after an IPO or SPAC listing; exceptions for spin-offs from existing constituents |
| Listing and domicile | Eligible U.S. companies listed on NYSE, Nasdaq or Cboe; ETFs, preferred shares and ADRs excluded |
| Sector representation | Consideration of GICS sector weights and the eligible U.S. large-cap market |

When does membership change? Scheduled changes are announced with the March, June, September and December quarterly rebalances and take effect before trading opens on the trading day after the third Friday of those months. Vacancies caused by acquisitions, spin-offs or bankruptcies are filled when needed, regardless of the quarter.

### Examples of changes driven by rules

- July 2002: Applying the U.S.-company requirement, seven non-U.S. constituents were removed together and replaced with seven U.S. companies, including five new listings. (Mondo Visione)
- June 2009: Covidien moved its domicile to Ireland and Tyco Electronics (TE) to Switzerland, losing eligibility and leaving the index. The criteria were later relaxed, and both returned in 2011.
- September 2008: During the financial crisis, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac left, while Salesforce and Fastenal joined. Lehman Brothers was removed shortly after filing for bankruptcy.
- Sears in 2012 and Sprint in 2013: Increased controlling-shareholder ownership reduced their public floats below the required level, leading to removal.
- June 2026: An exception allowing rapid inclusion of very large IPOs such as SpaceX and OpenAI was considered, but S&P DJI decided to retain all seasoning, profitability and IWF requirements. (S&P DJI consultation results)

## Types of deletion reasons

Three main reasons account for 90%: being acquired, scheduled replacement after shrinking in size, and structural changes following spin-offs. The following classification uses the original explanations in 414 change records, mostly from 2007–2026.

| Type | Count | Share | What happened | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mergers and acquisitions | 173 | 42% | A target is delisted or absorbed by another member, leaving a vacancy. Includes private-equity acquisitions that take a company private. | Dell MBO (2013); Amazon acquisition of Whole Foods (2017); Mars acquisition of Kellanova (2025); Paramount Skydance acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery (2026) |
| Scheduled rebalance (market capitalization) | 147 | 36% | Stocks losing large-cap representation as their prices fall move to the MidCap 400 or SmallCap 600, while larger stocks move up. | Eastman Kodak and New York Times out, Netflix in (2010); Bed Bath & Beyond (2017); American Airlines out, Palantir in (2024) |
| Splits and spin-offs | 51 | 12% | A business spun off from an existing member is added, with a smaller stock removed if needed. | Abbott spin-off of AbbVie (2013); GE HealthCare and GE Vernova (2023, 2024); FedEx Freight (2026) |
| Ticker or name change | 11 | 3% | Only the label changes, without an actual company replacement. | Kraft to Mondelez (2012); Ceridian to Dayforce (2024) |
| Share-class adjustment | 9 | 2% | Addition of a new class, such as Google Class C or Under Armour Class C. | Google GOOGL (2014) |
| Bankruptcy or resolution | 6 | 1% | Bankruptcy filing or FDIC receivership. | Lehman Brothers (2008); PG&E (2019); SVB, Signature and First Republic (2023) |
| Other eligibility loss | 9 | 2% | Foreign domicile moves: 3; insufficient float: 2; delisting: 1; insufficient size: 1; index-system restructuring: 2. | Covidien (2009); Sears (2012) |
| Unspecified or other | 8 | 2% | No reason in the original data or ambiguous classification. | — |

Two points deserve attention. First, reasons for additions are not listed separately: the committee fills vacancies with regard to sector balance and size. Second, the companies added and deleted on one row are not causally connected; they are simply the pair exchanging places on the same day.

During the M&A boom of 2015–2018, most deletions followed acquisitions. Since 2023, acquisition-related deletions have declined, while quarterly capitalization-based replacements of three or four companies have continued.

From 2020, scheduled rebalancing overtook M&A as the leading deletion reason. 2007–2019: M&A 123 versus rebalancing 66; 2020–2026: 40 versus 75. Original chart retained unchanged.

## Trends by era and notable constituent changes

The history records the shift in the center of U.S. industry from manufacturing and utilities to finance, and then to technology and AI infrastructure.

Wikipedia change table · 2007–October 2026 · 2026 through October

| Period | Trend | Notable additions | Notable deletions |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1957–1980s | Sector-quota era; 40 financial-sector places introduced in 1976 | Disney and Anheuser-Busch (1976), Intel (1976), Apple (1982), Oracle (1989) | Houston Natural Gas and Allegheny Energy (1976, utilities allocation reduced) |
| 1990s | Technology additions after quotas ended; sharp growth in financial M&A | Cisco (1993), Microsoft (1994), Yahoo (1999) | Amoco (1998, acquired by BP); General Re (1998, acquired by Berkshire) |
| 2000–2007 | Dot-com boom and collapse; removal of non-U.S. companies in 2002 | Starbucks (2000), Nvidia (2001), Amazon (2005), Google (2006) | Bethlehem Steel (2000); AT&T Corp. (2005, acquired by SBC) |
| 2008–2009 | Financial crisis | Salesforce and Fastenal (2008), Visa (2009) | Lehman Brothers, Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, Wachovia and Countrywide (2008) |
| 2010s | Rise of platforms and biotech; large acquisitions and successive spin-offs | Netflix (2010), BlackRock (2011), Facebook (2013), PayPal (2015) | Eastman Kodak (2010); Dell (2013, going private); Yahoo (2017, acquired by Verizon) |
| 2020–2022 | Pandemic and growth-stock strength | Tesla (2020, largest inclusion by size), Moderna (2021) | Macy’s and Harley-Davidson (2020); Twitter (2022, acquired by Musk) |
| 2023–2026 | Regional-bank crisis; AI infrastructure, fintech and private-market managers | Uber, Airbnb, Blackstone (2023); Palantir, Dell (2024); Coinbase, Robinhood (2025); Vertiv, Marvell, Reddit (2026) | SVB, Signature, First Republic (2023); Walgreens (2025); Electronic Arts (2026) |

Addition dates use the current constituent list’s Date added field. Nvidia (2001-11-30), Microsoft (1994-06-01) and Apple (1982-11-30) have no corresponding rows in the change table, so their dates were checked in the constituent list.

### Companies that left and returned — deletion is not a permanent sentence

| Company | Deletion | Return |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dell | 2013 management buyout and going private | September 2024 |
| AMD | September 2013, size-related removal | March 2017 |
| Ciena | December 2009, size-related removal | February 2026 |
| Illumina | June 2024, size-related removal | September 2026 |
| Sandisk | 2016 acquisition by Western Digital | November 2025 following its spin-off |
| Covidien | June 2009, eligibility loss following Irish redomiciliation | February 2011 after domicile criteria were relaxed |

## Detailed recent changes (2025–October 2026)

Of the 42 change rows since 2025, 24 are scheduled rebalances, 13 mergers and acquisitions, and five spin-offs. When a spun-off entity joins, deletion-only rows may follow a few days later to restore the stock count to 500 (Corteva, Conagra, EPAM, CarMax and Eastman Chemical). Changes for 2023–2024 and earlier are all in the Excel file.
